classification.difficultyReason: Apply restricted digit counts and divisibility tests, then combine the preceding single-digit and intersection probabilities using the addition rule.

content.prompt: A three-digit number is formed from the digits 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 (no repetitions allowed). Find the probability that:

answer.worked:
There are ${}^{5}P_3=5\times4\times3=60$ possible numbers, all equally likely. Only one is 473.
$$P(473)=\frac{1}{60}.$$

The last digit is 3, 5 or 7: three choices. The other two positions have ${}^{4}P_2=4\times3$ arrangements.
$$P(\text{odd})=\frac{3\times4\times3}{60}=\frac35.$$

The last digit must be 5. There are ${}^{4}P_2=4\times3$ ways to fill the other two positions.
$$P(\text{divisible by }5)=\frac{4\times3}{60}=\frac15.$$

The digit sum must be divisible by 3. The valid sets are $\{3,4,5\}$, $\{3,5,7\}$, $\{4,5,6\}$ and $\{5,6,7\}$. Each has $3!$ arrangements.
$$P(\text{divisible by }3)=\frac{4\times3!}{60}=\frac25.$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: the number starts with 4 and ends with 7,

answer.worked:
The middle digit can be 3, 5 or 6.
$$P(\text{starts with }4\text{ and ends with }7)=\frac3{60}=\frac1{20}.$$

Without 3, the digits are chosen and arranged from four remaining digits.
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{contains }3)&=1-\frac{{}^{4}P_3}{60}\\&=1-\frac{4\times3\times2}{60}\\&=\frac35.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: g
children.prompt: the number contains the digits 3 and 5,

answer.worked:
Choose one of three positions for 3, then one of two positions for 5. The remaining digit is 4, 6 or 7.
$$P(\text{contains }3\text{ and }5)=\frac{3\times2\times3}{60}=\frac3{10}.$$

children.label: h
children.prompt: the number contains the digits 3 or 5,

answer.worked:
Let $A$ mean the number contains 3 and $B$ mean it contains 5. By symmetry, $P(B)=P(A)=\frac35$. Using parts f and g,
$$\begin{aligned}P(A\cup B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\\&=\frac35+\frac35-\frac3{10}\\&=\frac9{10}.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: all digits in the number are odd,

answer.worked:
The digits must be 3, 5 and 7, arranged in $3!$ ways.
$$P(\text{all digits odd})=\frac{3!}{60}=\frac1{10}.$$

The first digit is 5, 6 or 7: three choices. There are ${}^{4}P_2$ ways to fill the other two positions.
$$P(\text{greater than }500)=\frac{3\times4\times3}{60}=\frac35.$$
